transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, yes, thank you for fitting me in. Um, well, to be completely honest, I came in because I just feel so incredibly worn out all the time. And I don't mean just the normal 'oh, it's been a busy week' kind of tired. It's this deep, heavy exhaustion that never really leaves. Like, I can spend a full, solid night in bed—eight or nine hours, doing everything right—and when I wake up, my body literally feels like it's made of sandbags. Just total dead weight. 

It's making everything so hard. Getting through a normal workday... I'm a market research analyst, so I really need to be sharp and focused on data and campaign metrics, but lately, just sitting at my desk and trying to get through my reports takes absolutely everything I have. And it's not even just the mental toll at work, it's the physical stuff at home, too. Like, the other day I was staring at a basket of clean clothes, and just the thought of folding the laundry felt impossible. Lifting my arms to fold a shirt felt like I was trying to move mountains. I just don't understand why I have zero energy, no matter how much I rest, and it's just really starting to impact every single part of my day, from the minute I wake up to the minute I finally just give up and go back to sleep.
Have you been feeling sad or down most of the time lately?

Well... yeah. Honestly, yes. It's not just the physical tiredness, though I guess they kind of feed into each other. It's this... I don't know how to explain it perfectly, but most days, almost every single day lately, I wake up and before I even throw the covers off, there's just this heavy, flat feeling right here in the center of my chest. Like someone poured lead in there overnight. 

And I'll drag myself up, go to the kitchen, maybe make a cup of coffee—which I don't even really want half the time, I just make it out of pure routine hoping the caffeine will spark something, anything—and I'll just sit there at the kitchen table. We have this big window that looks out over the backyard, and I'll just sit there with both hands on my mug while it gets completely cold, just staring out at the yard for I don't even know how long. The neighbor's dog might be barking, or the wind is blowing the trees around, and I just feel so... nothing. 

And while I'm sitting there staring, it's just this overwhelming sense that... well, I look ahead, and I truly feel like there is no good version of the future coming. You know? Like, what is the point of going to work, or analyzing another dataset, or even folding those clothes, when everything just feels so incredibly bleak? It's not always a crying kind of sad, it's more just this suffocating flatness where I can't picture anything ever getting better or feeling lighter. I used to be able to look forward to things, but now I just sit at that table and think, 'This is it. This is just how it's going to be.' It's really hard to shake.
Do you find yourself enjoying things you used to like, or has that changed recently?

It’s definitely changed. I mean, it’s changed a lot. And it’s funny you ask that, because my sister was just asking me the same thing the other day, and I didn't even really know how to answer her without sounding ungrateful or just completely lazy. But the truth is, I just don't care about the things I used to love. 

Like, I used to be such an active person. I would make time, no matter how busy work got with campaigns or whatever, I would always carve out time for hiking on the weekends. There's this trail about forty minutes from my house, the one that goes up past the old reservoir, and I used to go up there almost every Sunday morning. I loved it. And I was doing yoga three times a week, just in my living room, but I was really dedicated to it. Plus my garden... I have these raised beds in the backyard, the ones I stare at from the kitchen window now, and I used to spend hours out there weeding and planting. I even got really into bird photography a couple of years ago. I bought this beautiful, ridiculously expensive telephoto lens so I could capture the blue jays and the cardinals that come to the feeder. 

But lately? I just... I can't. I keep making plans to go hike with my friends, and then Friday night rolls around and I just text them some excuse and cancel. My camera is literally just sitting in its case in the hall closet collecting dust. The garden is completely overgrown with weeds, and I just look at it and feel nothing. I used to get so much joy out of getting a perfect shot of a bird taking off, or finally getting a tricky yoga pose right, but now... I just think about getting the camera out, or rolling out the mat, and it just doesn't feel worth the effort. It’s like, why bother? What’s the point? It’s not going to make me feel any better anyway. So I just don't do any of it anymore.
How long have you been feeling this way?

Well, let me think... it's been a while now. I mean, the really heavy, depressed part—the feeling like I'm moving through molasses and just being completely exhausted all the time—that's been going on for, I'd say, about the past two months. Most days, anyway. 

I actually remember exactly when it started to get really bad, because it was right around the time we were launching this massive Q3 campaign at work. It was supposed to be this huge, exciting project, and normally I'd be all over the data, digging into the demographics and the click-through rates. But I just remember sitting in this big kickoff meeting, and my boss was talking, and I just felt this wave of... I don't even know, just total emptiness and fatigue wash over me. And I thought, 'Oh, I'm just burnt out from the Q2 push, I just need a weekend to sleep.' But then the weekend passed, and I slept, and it didn't go away. 

And then the next week came, and it was the same thing. And it just kept going. I started tracking it a little bit in my head, you know, like, 'Okay, Tuesday was bad, Wednesday was terrible, Thursday I barely made it through.' And before I knew it, it had been weeks. And now we're here, and it's been two solid months of just... this. Two months of waking up and feeling like I haven't slept in a year. Two months of staring out that kitchen window. It feels like a lot longer, honestly, when you're in the middle of it, but yeah, looking at the calendar, it's been about two months of this really intense, slowed-down feeling.
Are there any activities that you still find pleasure in or look forward to?

I mean... honestly? No. I really can't think of a single thing. And it's so frustrating because, like I was saying before about the hiking and the yoga and the garden... I used to have so many things that I genuinely loved doing. My weekends were packed. I’d be up at 6 AM, getting my gear together, checking the weather app to see if the lighting was going to be good for the bird photos. I’d have my thermos of coffee, my boots by the door, and I'd be so excited to get out there. I used to feel this... this rush, you know? When you finally spot a cardinal through the lens and get the focus just right. Or when you finally pull the last weed out of a garden bed and look at the fresh dirt. 

But now... I don't know, it's just like a switch flipped. I keep trying to force it. Like, I’ll tell myself, 'Okay, this weekend, you are going to take the camera out. You are going to go to the reservoir.' And I'll even get as far as taking the camera case out of the closet. I’ll set it on the kitchen counter. And I'll just look at it. And the thought of actually unzipping the case, checking the battery, putting on my hiking boots, driving the forty minutes... it just feels like climbing Mount Everest. It just feels so utterly pointless. 

So I don't do it. I just leave the camera on the counter for three days until I finally put it back in the closet so I don't have to look at it anymore. I keep canceling on my friends, too. They’ll text me on Thursday, 'Hey, still on for the trail on Saturday?' and I’ll just stare at my phone, trying to muster up even an ounce of enthusiasm, and there's just nothing there. It's just blank. So I type out some excuse about work being crazy or having a migraine, and I just stay home. It’s like all the color has been drained out of everything I used to enjoy, and I just can't find a reason to put the effort in anymore.
Have you had any thoughts of not wanting to be alive or wishing you could just disappear?

Well... I mean, it's hard to talk about, honestly. But since you're asking... yeah. I have. Not all the time, but... mostly at night. It's always at night, when the house is quiet and my husband is asleep next to me, and I'm just lying there awake, staring at the ceiling, feeling that heavy, molasses feeling I told you about. 

My husband, he's so good, you know? He tries so hard. He's been picking up all the slack around the house, doing the dishes, trying to get me to eat, listening to me cancel on my friends... and I just look at him sleeping, and I start thinking... I catch myself thinking that maybe he'd just be better off without me. Because right now, I'm just this weight pulling him down. I'm not the woman he married, the one who was always up at dawn, excited about life. I'm just this... empty shell sitting on the couch. 

And the thought just kind of creeps in, like, 'If I wasn't here, he wouldn't have to deal with this anymore. He could have a normal life. He could find someone who actually wants to go hiking with him, someone who doesn't just stare blankly at a camera case for three days.' And it's not like... I want to be clear, I haven't made a plan or anything. I'm not sitting there figuring out how to do it. I don't have, like, a specific method in mind or anything like that. But the thought... the thought of just slipping away, of just disappearing so I wouldn't be a burden anymore... it just keeps coming back. It keeps circling the drain in my mind, especially around 2 or 3 AM when everything feels the darkest. And it happens enough now that... it actually really scares me. Because I never used to think like that. Never. But now it's just this recurring loop in my head late at night.
Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight recently?

Weight... well, I haven't actually stepped on a scale in... gosh, it has to be since before that Q3 campaign started. I used to be pretty meticulous about it, you know? Being a data person, I like tracking things, so I’d weigh myself every Friday morning right before my shower, just to keep an eye on things. When you sit at a desk analyzing market trends all day, it’s easy to get a little stagnant if you aren't careful, so I liked having the numbers. 

But lately... I just haven't even thought to look at the scale. It's just gathering dust in the corner of the bathroom. And like I mentioned before, my husband has been doing most of the cooking, and I just kind of eat whatever he puts in front of me. He'll make these nice dinners, and I'll eat them just so he doesn't worry, but I'm not really paying attention to portions or calories or anything like I used to. 

And as for my clothes... I'm mostly just living in these old gray sweatpants these days. The thought of putting on real pants with a button and a zipper just feels like entirely too much effort. They have a drawstring, so it's not like they're a great gauge of whether I've gained or lost anything. I did have to put on a pair of regular jeans last week when I finally dragged myself to the pharmacy, and... I mean, I guess they felt normal? Maybe a little loose, or maybe a little tight because I haven't been hiking and I'm just sitting on the couch all day... I honestly couldn't even tell you. 

It’s strange, really. You'd think with how completely different I feel on the inside, how heavy and entirely drained I am, that there would be some physical proof of it on the outside. But... no. As far as I can tell, my body is just staying exactly the same. So, no, I haven't noticed any major changes either way.
Have you noticed yourself moving more slowly than usual or feeling like you're speeding up in your thoughts or actions?

Speeding up? Oh, gosh, no. I wish I had even a fraction of that kind of energy right now, honestly. No, it's... it's the exact opposite of speeding up. 

Actually, my husband brought this up just the other day. We were in the kitchen, and I was trying to make a cup of tea, which usually takes me two minutes, but I was just sort of standing there holding the mug. And he was watching me, and he finally just gently took the mug out of my hand and said that I move around the house like I am underwater. And when he said that, it really clicked for me, because that is exactly what it feels like. It feels like the air in our house has turned into this thick, heavy fluid, and just the act of lifting my arm to open a cabinet door or walking from the living room to the bathroom takes this monumental, exhausting physical effort. Every movement is just so incredibly labored.

And it's not just my body, either. It's my talking, too. He'll ask me something so incredibly simple, like... oh, yesterday, he asked if I wanted him to pick up Thai food or pizza for dinner. Just a basic, everyday question, right? But I just stood there looking at him. I could hear the question perfectly fine, I knew what he was asking, but my brain... it was like the gears were just completely rusted shut. It can take me a while to answer because the words just come out so slowly. I have to physically think about forming the answer in my head, and then it's like I have to force the signal down to my mouth to actually speak it out loud. 

And he's just standing there waiting for me to say 'pizza', and I can see this look of concern on his face, but I just can't make myself respond any faster. It's incredibly frustrating because, you know, in my job, I have to be sharp. I analyze market trends, I have to present data in these big strategy meetings, I have to think on my feet and answer rapid-fire questions from the marketing directors. I'm used to being quick. And right now, I can barely answer my own husband about dinner without taking a full minute just to get a single word out of my mouth. So, yeah, everything is just... painfully slow.
Do you feel like your thoughts are moving slowly as well, or is it just your physical movements that feel sluggish?

Oh, it's definitely my thoughts too. Honestly, maybe even more so than the physical part, if you can believe it. I mean, I'm a market research analyst, so my entire livelihood depends on my ability to process information quickly, you know? My whole day is about looking at data, finding patterns, drawing conclusions, and communicating that to the marketing directors. But lately... it's like my brain is just wading through thick mud. 

Just the other day, I was sitting at my desk—well, my home office desk, since I've been trying to work from home to just hide how much I'm struggling—and I had this client email open. And attached to it were these survey results from a recent campaign we ran. I must have read that same email, and the same paragraph of those survey results, three, maybe four times. I was staring right at the words, tracking them with my eyes, but I just could not absorb it. Nothing was sticking. The information would just bounce right off my brain, like I was reading a foreign language I didn't understand. 

And the decision-making... oh my gosh, it's completely shot. I'll sit there looking at my monitor, and I'll know I have a mountain of tasks I need to get through, but even just choosing which spreadsheet to open first can feel weirdly impossible. Like, a genuinely monumental task. Should I open the Q3 projections? Should I look at the demographic breakdown? I just sit there staring at the little Excel icons on my desktop for twenty minutes because my brain just won't process the next logical step. It's so incredibly frustrating because I've been doing this for years, and I know exactly how to run these analyses. I used to be able to juggle three different client accounts in my head at once, remembering all the little details, and now I'm just sitting there paralyzed, completely overwhelmed by the thought of double-clicking a file. So, yes, the slowness is absolutely in my head, too. It's like the spark that connects one thought to the next is just completely burned out.
Have you been feeling restless or having an urge to move around more than usual?

Right now? Oh, heavens no. Like I said, I'm practically glued to the couch and moving like molasses. But... well, actually, before this whole heavy, underwater feeling set in, it was a completely different story. It’s almost comical how different it was. 

Before all this, I had this... this intense burst where I just absolutely could not sit still. It was like I had a motor humming inside me that just wouldn't shut off. My husband would be trying to wind down for the evening and watch a movie, and I’d sit down on the sofa next to him for maybe two minutes before I was just springing right back up again. I kept jumping up to do things. Like, I decided, completely out of nowhere, that my home office was entirely inefficient for my workflow. So I was up sketching out these elaborate new office layouts on this old graphing paper I dug out of a drawer somewhere. I was measuring the desk, measuring the distance to the windows, thinking about the glare on my monitors and how I could optimize the space... 

And then I started reorganizing all my files. Not just the physical papers in the filing cabinet, which I also did, but my entire digital directory for work. I was color-coding folders and renaming sub-directories at all hours of the night. It was just this constant, driving urge to start one more task, and then just one more, even when there was absolutely no real reason it had to happen right then. The work deadlines were already met, it was late, but I was just buzzing around the house, picking up a new project before I even finished the last one. I just had to be doing something, moving somehow, fixing something. It drove my husband a little crazy, I think, because I just wouldn't stop pacing and rearranging things. So, yes, I definitely had that urge to move, but... well, obviously, that energy is completely gone now.
Have you lost interest in activities for at least two weeks?

Oh, absolutely. It’s been... gosh, definitely longer than two weeks at this point. It’s honestly so sad to think about, because I usually have so many things I love doing outside of work. I mean, sitting at a desk looking at market research data all day means I really need a creative and physical outlet, you know? So I usually make time for all sorts of things. Hiking, my evening yoga classes, working in my garden... I planted all these heirloom tomatoes and bell peppers this spring, and I was so excited about them. 

And my absolute favorite thing is taking bird photos. I have this gorgeous camera with a huge telephoto lens that I saved up for, and I used to spend hours out on the trails early in the morning just waiting for the perfect shot of a cedar waxwing or a cardinal. It was my way to completely decompress. 

But lately... I don't know, I just don't care about any of it. At all. I keep canceling my yoga classes, which I feel awful about because the instructor is so sweet, but I just can't make myself go. And my camera is just sitting in its bag in the hall closet, totally untouched for weeks. I see it when I open the door to get my coat, and I just feel... nothing. No spark, no desire to pick it up. Even the garden, I just look out the kitchen window at it, and I know the weeds are probably taking over, but none of it feels worth the effort. Everything that used to bring me joy just feels like this massive, pointless chore now. It's like the color has been completely drained out of my life, and I just can't find a single reason to bother with any of it.
Have you lost a significant amount of weight over the past two months?

Weight? Um, no, not that I've noticed. I mean, I haven't really been on a scale lately, to be completely honest with you. It's just not something I've been tracking. You'd think, with how little I've been moving, maybe I'd be gaining weight, but I just... I haven't really been paying attention to my body in that way. 

My husband usually does most of the cooking, and he's been trying to make these really nice, healthy dinners for us—salmon and roasted vegetables, things like that—because he knows I'm struggling. And I do eat it, mostly just because he put it in front of me and I don't want to hurt his feelings, but I'm not really tasting it, you know? It's just fuel. I'm just chewing and swallowing because that's what you're supposed to do. 

But as for actually losing a significant amount of weight... no, my clothes still fit exactly the same. My work trousers, the few times I've actually put them on instead of just wearing sweatpants all day, they don't feel any looser. So, no, I don't think my weight has really changed much at all over the last couple of months. It's just... stagnant. Like everything else right now.
Have you been feeling an internal restlessness or an urge to move around more than usual recently?

Restless? Oh, no, not right now. Like I was saying earlier about feeling glued to the couch... it's actually the exact opposite of restless right now. It's funny you ask about moving around more than usual, because my husband, bless his heart, he actually brought this up just the other day. We were sitting in the living room—well, I was sitting, he was tidying up—and he stopped and just looked at me. He said, "Honey, you look like you're moving underwater." And he's right. Every single movement feels like I'm pushing through wet cement. Just lifting my arm to reach for my tea mug feels like this monumental, exhausting effort. 

And it's not just the physical moving, either. It's... it's my whole brain, my speech. He’ll ask me something incredibly simple, like, "Do you want chicken or fish for dinner?" or "Did you see where I put the mail?" and I just sit there. I hear the words, I know what they mean, but getting my mouth to form a response... it takes so long. The words just come out so incredibly slowly, if they come out at all. I have to think about taking a breath, forming the sound, pushing it out... it's exhausting. I feel like I'm on a completely different time delay than the rest of the world. So, no, definitely no urge to move around right now. It's more like I've just ground to an absolute halt.
Do you feel like your thoughts and movements have slowed down significantly over the past two months?

Yeah, exactly. Like I was just saying a minute ago, it’s exactly that. The slowing down is... well, it’s profound, really. Over the past couple of months, it’s just gotten so much worse. When my husband pointed out that I look like I’m moving underwater, it honestly hit me pretty hard, because you know how sometimes you feel a certain way but you aren't sure if anyone else can actually see it? Well, he sees it. It’s impossible to miss. Just walking down the hallway to get a glass of water feels like I have lead weights tied to my ankles, and I have to actively think about picking up one foot and putting it in front of the other. 

And the thoughts... gosh, it’s so frustrating. Like I mentioned with him asking me those simple questions about dinner. It’s not just that I’m ignoring him, it’s that my brain literally feels like it’s wading through thick syrup. I’ll sit there, and I know I need to say 'chicken' or 'the mail is on the counter,' but the connection between my brain and my mouth is just... lagging. Like a terrible internet connection on a work video call. I used to be so sharp, you know? I analyze market data for a living, I have to be quick on my feet, finding trends and pulling reports and presenting them. And now... just getting the words out to answer a basic yes or no question in my own living room takes me so incredibly long. The words just drag out of me. It’s embarrassing, honestly, to just sit there staring blankly at your own husband while you try to force a single, simple sentence out of your mouth. So yes, significantly slowed down. In every possible way.
Have you made any plans or taken any steps towards acting on those thoughts of not wanting to be alive?

Plans? No. No, I haven't... I haven't actually made any plans. I haven't taken any steps, like buying anything or... or writing anything down. It's not like that. But... it's just that the thoughts are there, you know? Especially late at night. That's when it's the worst. My husband will be asleep next to me, and he's just so peaceful, and he's been working so hard to take care of me, making those dinners and trying to keep the house running while I just sit there like a lump. And I'll just lie there in the dark, staring at the ceiling, and this thought just creeps in... this really heavy, awful thought that maybe he'd just be better off without me. 

Because right now, I'm just a burden, aren't I? I'm dragging him down. He didn't sign up for this, to be married to a ghost who can barely form a sentence or get off the couch. And I think about how much easier his life would be, how much lighter it would be, if he didn't have to worry about me anymore. If he didn't have to come home from work and immediately start caretaking. 

I haven't figured out a way to... to do it. I haven't sat down and plotted anything out. But it's just that the thought keeps coming back. It's like a record skipping in my head. 'He'd be better off, he'd be better off.' And it scares me. It really does scare me, because I don't want to hurt him, but then my brain tells me that staying around is what's actually hurting him. It's so confusing and it's so dark in my head at 2 AM. But as for actual steps? No. Just... just the thoughts. But they're there enough that I'm frightened of my own mind sometimes.
Have you lost a noticeable amount of weight recently?

Weight? Um, no, not that I've noticed. I mean, I haven't been on a scale recently, honestly. The thought of even going into the bathroom and pulling the scale out from under the sink just feels like way too much effort right now, like everything else. But my clothes don't feel any looser. If anything, they might feel a little tighter, maybe? Because, like I said, I'm just sitting on the couch all day. I'm not moving. 

My husband has been trying to get me to eat, making those dinners I mentioned, the chicken or fish or whatever he decides on because I can't make a choice. And I'll eat some of it, mostly just to appease him, because I can see how hard he's trying and I feel so guilty. The food tastes like cardboard, honestly. I don't have an appetite, not really. Chewing just feels like a chore. But I force it down. And then I just go back to sitting. Or lying down. 

I used to go to the gym, you know. I had this whole routine before work. I'd get up at 5:30, go to the spin class, shower there, and be at my desk by 8:00, ready to dive into the market reports. I was so active. I liked feeling strong. And now... now I can barely walk down the hall. So, no, I haven't lost weight. I'm just... stagnant. Just sitting here, taking up space, not burning a single calorie. It's just another thing that makes me feel awful about myself, to be honest. But no, no noticeable weight loss. Just the opposite of being active.
Have you thought about how you would end your life if you decided to act on those thoughts?

How I would do it? Um... well, like I was trying to explain before, it's not that I've sat down and figured out the logistics of it. I haven't... I haven't picked a method or thought about the actual steps of ending it. It's more just this overwhelming, suffocating feeling. Especially late at night, like I mentioned. That's really when the house is so quiet, and the darkness just kind of presses in on me. I'll be lying there, and my husband is right next to me, sleeping so peacefully, completely unaware of the storm going on in my head. And I just catch myself thinking, over and over, that he might just be better off without me. 

It's just... it's a terrifying thought, but it's also strangely persistent. It's like a loop that just plays in my mind when I can't sleep. I think about all the extra work he's doing, all the stress I'm causing him, how I'm just this heavy weight dragging him down. And the thought just creeps in: 'If I wasn't here, he wouldn't have to deal with this.' I haven't made a plan. I really haven't. I haven't thought about pills or... or anything else. I don't know how I would actually do it. But the thought just keeps coming back, night after night. It comes back enough that it really scares me. It scares me that my brain is even going there, that it sees my absence as some kind of solution or relief for him. So no, no specific method or plan, just... just this awful, recurring thought that won't leave me alone when the lights go out.
Do you feel like you're moving more quickly or slowly than usual?

Slowly. Definitely, unequivocally slowly. It's actually... well, my husband just brought this up the other day. He was in the kitchen, making one of those dinners I told you about, and I had finally managed to force myself off the couch just to get a glass of water. Which, honestly, even just standing up feels like I'm wearing a lead suit these days. 

Anyway, he was watching me walk across the living room, and he pointed out that I move around the house like I am underwater. And when he said it, it resonated so much because that is exactly what it feels like. It's like the air in our house has suddenly turned into thick syrup or molasses, and every single movement requires this monumental, exhausting push against the current. Just lifting my arm to open the cabinet door feels heavy. 

And it's not just my body, either. It's my speech. He'll ask me something incredibly simple, you know, something that shouldn't require any real brainpower, like, "Do you want peas or broccoli with this?" or "Did you see where I put the mail?" And I hear the question, the sound registers in my ears, but it's like it gets stuck somewhere in the fog in my brain. It can take me a while to answer him because the words just come out so slowly. I have to search for them, and then I have to physically force my mouth to form them, syllable by syllable. 

It's so frustrating because, like I said, I used to be so sharp. In market research, you have to be quick on your feet, you're constantly analyzing data, spitting out reports, talking a mile a minute in meetings. I was always the one walking fast down the office hallways. Now, I just sit there staring at my husband while he waits for me to answer a basic question about vegetables, and my brain is just moving at a glacial pace. The words just drag. Everything just drags. It really does feel like I'm just submerged at the bottom of a pool, trying to function through all that water pressure.
Do you think your depression is mild, moderate, or severe?

Moderate, I think. If I had to put a label on it, I'd say moderate. I mean, it's definitely not mild. Mild sounds like... like a bad weekend or just feeling a little blue because it's raining, you know? Mild is something you can just shake off with a good cup of coffee or a brisk walk. And obviously, I can't do that. The coffee just sits there getting cold because I can't bring myself to drink it, and we already talked about the walking. 

But I also hesitate to say severe. Severe sounds like... I don't know, like I'm completely catatonic or like I need to be in a hospital, which I don't think I do. I mean, I'm still here, right? I'm sitting in this chair, talking to you. I'm forcing down the chicken my husband makes. I'm not... I'm not completely gone. I'm still functioning on some very, very basic, primitive level, even if it feels like I'm doing it underwater. 

So, moderate feels right. It's this heavy, suffocating middle ground. It's bad enough that I can't work, which is devastating because my job was my whole identity. I loved the market research, the fast pace, the data. And now I can't even look at a spreadsheet without feeling completely overwhelmed. It's bad enough that I'm dragging my husband down with me, making him worry and take on all the household chores. But it's not so bad that I've completely lost touch with reality or that I've, you know, actually made a plan to do anything drastic, like we talked about. It's just this constant, exhausting, moderate weight that I'm carrying around every single day, from the moment I wake up until I finally manage to fall asleep. It's just... it's a lot. But yeah, moderate is probably the right word for it.

Like, I can spend a full, solid night in bed—eight or nine hours, doing everything right—and when I wake up, my body literally feels like it's made of sandbags. Just total dead weight.

But lately? I just... I can't. I keep making plans to go hike with my friends, and then Friday night rolls around and I just text them some excuse and cancel. My camera is literally just sitting in its case in the hall closet collecting dust. The garden is completely overgrown with weeds, and I just look at it and feel nothing. I used to get so much joy out of getting a perfect shot of a bird taking off, or finally getting a tricky yoga pose right, but now... Like a terrible internet connection on a work video call. I used to be so sharp, you know? I analyze market data for a living, I have to be quick on my feet, finding trends and pulling reports and presenting them. And now... just getting the words out to answer a basic yes or no question in my own living room takes me so incredibly long. The words just drag out of me. It’s embarrassing, honestly, to just sit there staring blankly at your own husband while you try to force a single, simple sentence out of your mouth. So yes, significantly slowed down. In every possible way.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of suicidal thoughts with a plan
doctor.question: Have you made any plans or taken any steps towards acting on those thoughts of not wanting to be alive?

target_item.name: Death_Suicide
target_item.manifestation: Late at night I catch myself thinking my husband might be better off without me, and even though I have not made a plan, the thought keeps coming back enough that it scares me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about suicidal plans or steps towards ending my life, which directly corresponds to the symptom of death/suicidal thoughts.

patient.answer:
Plans? No. No, I haven't... I haven't actually made any plans. I haven't taken any steps, like buying anything or... or writing anything down. It's not like that. But... it's just that the thoughts are there, you know? Especially late at night. That's when it's the worst. My husband will be asleep next to me, and he's just so peaceful, and he's been working so hard to take care of me, making those dinners and trying to keep the house running while I just sit there like a lump. And I'll just lie there in the dark, staring at the ceiling, and this thought just creeps in... this really heavy, awful thought that maybe he'd just be better off without me. 

Because right now, I'm just a burden, aren't I? I'm dragging him down. He didn't sign up for this, to be married to a ghost who can barely form a sentence or get off the couch. And I think about how much easier his life would be, how much lighter it would be, if he didn't have to worry about me anymore. If he didn't have to come home from work and immediately start caretaking. 

I haven't figured out a way to... to do it. I haven't sat down and plotted anything out. But it's just that the thought keeps coming back. It's like a record skipping in my head. 'He'd be better off, he'd be better off.' And it scares me. It really does scare me, because I don't want to hurt him, but then my brain tells me that staying around is what's actually hurting him. It's so confusing and it's so dark in my head at 2 AM. But as for actual steps? No. Just... just the thoughts. But they're there enough that I'm frightened of my own mind sometimes.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of significant weight loss
doctor.question: Have you lost a noticeable amount of weight recently?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about recent noticeable weight loss, which corresponds to changes in weight or appetite. My symptom profile does not include an item for weight loss or appetite changes.

patient.answer:
Weight? Um, no, not that I've noticed. I mean, I haven't been on a scale recently, honestly. The thought of even going into the bathroom and pulling the scale out from under the sink just feels like way too much effort right now, like everything else. But my clothes don't feel any looser. If anything, they might feel a little tighter, maybe? Because, like I said, I'm just sitting on the couch all day. I'm not moving. 

My husband has been trying to get me to eat, making those dinners I mentioned, the chicken or fish or whatever he decides on because I can't make a choice. And I'll eat some of it, mostly just to appease him, because I can see how hard he's trying and I feel so guilty. The food tastes like cardboard, honestly. I don't have an appetite, not really. Chewing just feels like a chore. But I force it down. And then I just go back to sitting. Or lying down. 

I used to go to the gym, you know. I had this whole routine before work. I'd get up at 5:30, go to the spin class, shower there, and be at my desk by 8:00, ready to dive into the market reports. I was so active. I liked feeling strong. And now... now I can barely walk down the hall. So, no, I haven't lost weight. I'm just... stagnant. Just sitting here, taking up space, not burning a single calorie. It's just another thing that makes me feel awful about myself, to be honest. But no, no noticeable weight loss. Just the opposite of being active.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of suicidal ideation with a plan
doctor.question: Have you thought about how you would end your life if you decided to act on those thoughts?

target_item.name: Death_Suicide
target_item.manifestation: Late at night I catch myself thinking my husband might be better off without me, and even though I have not made a plan, the thought keeps coming back enough that it scares me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a specific plan or method for suicide, which falls under suicidal ideation.

patient.answer:
How I would do it? Um... well, like I was trying to explain before, it's not that I've sat down and figured out the logistics of it. I haven't... I haven't picked a method or thought about the actual steps of ending it. It's more just this overwhelming, suffocating feeling. Especially late at night, like I mentioned. That's really when the house is so quiet, and the darkness just kind of presses in on me. I'll be lying there, and my husband is right next to me, sleeping so peacefully, completely unaware of the storm going on in my head. And I just catch myself thinking, over and over, that he might just be better off without me. 

It's just... it's a terrifying thought, but it's also strangely persistent. It's like a loop that just plays in my mind when I can't sleep. I think about all the extra work he's doing, all the stress I'm causing him, how I'm just this heavy weight dragging him down. And the thought just creeps in: 'If I wasn't here, he wouldn't have to deal with this.' I haven't made a plan. I really haven't. I haven't thought about pills or... or anything else. I don't know how I would actually do it. But the thought just keeps coming back, night after night. It comes back enough that it really scares me. It scares me that my brain is even going there, that it sees my absence as some kind of solution or relief for him. So no, no specific method or plan, just... just this awful, recurring thought that won't leave me alone when the lights go out.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of psychomotor agitation or retardation
doctor.question: Do you feel like you're moving more quickly or slowly than usual?

target_item.name: Psychomotor_Changes
target_item.manifestation: My husband has pointed out that I move around the house like I am underwater, and when he asks me something simple it can take me a while to answer because the words come out so slowly.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about changes in my movement speed (moving more quickly or slowly), which directly corresponds to psychomotor changes.

patient.answer:
Slowly. Definitely, unequivocally slowly. It's actually... well, my husband just brought this up the other day. He was in the kitchen, making one of those dinners I told you about, and I had finally managed to force myself off the couch just to get a glass of water. Which, honestly, even just standing up feels like I'm wearing a lead suit these days. 

Anyway, he was watching me walk across the living room, and he pointed out that I move around the house like I am underwater. And when he said it, it resonated so much because that is exactly what it feels like. It's like the air in our house has suddenly turned into thick syrup or molasses, and every single movement requires this monumental, exhausting push against the current. Just lifting my arm to open the cabinet door feels heavy. 

And it's not just my body, either. It's my speech. He'll ask me something incredibly simple, you know, something that shouldn't require any real brainpower, like, "Do you want peas or broccoli with this?" or "Did you see where I put the mail?" And I hear the question, the sound registers in my ears, but it's like it gets stuck somewhere in the fog in my brain. It can take me a while to answer him because the words just come out so slowly. I have to search for them, and then I have to physically force my mouth to form them, syllable by syllable. 

It's so frustrating because, like I said, I used to be so sharp. In market research, you have to be quick on your feet, you're constantly analyzing data, spitting out reports, talking a mile a minute in meetings. I was always the one walking fast down the office hallways. Now, I just sit there staring at my husband while he waits for me to answer a basic question about vegetables, and my brain is just moving at a glacial pace. The words just drag. Everything just drags. It really does feel like I'm just submerged at the bottom of a pool, trying to function through all that water pressure.

doctor.intent: Determine the severity of depressive episode
doctor.question: Do you think your depression is mild, moderate, or severe?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking for a self-assessment of the severity of the depression (mild, moderate, or severe), which is not explicitly covered by any specific symptom item in the profile.

patient.answer:
Moderate, I think. If I had to put a label on it, I'd say moderate. I mean, it's definitely not mild. Mild sounds like... like a bad weekend or just feeling a little blue because it's raining, you know? Mild is something you can just shake off with a good cup of coffee or a brisk walk. And obviously, I can't do that. The coffee just sits there getting cold because I can't bring myself to drink it, and we already talked about the walking. 

But I also hesitate to say severe. Severe sounds like... I don't know, like I'm completely catatonic or like I need to be in a hospital, which I don't think I do. I mean, I'm still here, right? I'm sitting in this chair, talking to you. I'm forcing down the chicken my husband makes. I'm not... I'm not completely gone. I'm still functioning on some very, very basic, primitive level, even if it feels like I'm doing it underwater. 

So, moderate feels right. It's this heavy, suffocating middle ground. It's bad enough that I can't work, which is devastating because my job was my whole identity. I loved the market research, the fast pace, the data. And now I can't even look at a spreadsheet without feeling completely overwhelmed. It's bad enough that I'm dragging my husband down with me, making him worry and take on all the household chores. But it's not so bad that I've completely lost touch with reality or that I've, you know, actually made a plan to do anything drastic, like we talked about. It's just this constant, exhausting, moderate weight that I'm carrying around every single day, from the moment I wake up until I finally manage to fall asleep. It's just... it's a lot. But yeah, moderate is probably the right word for it.
